newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-3i NAV rises more slowly in 1996/7.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-3i NAV rises more slowly in 1996/7.

text.p: British investment company 3i Group Plc on Thursday reported a 14.1 percent increase in its net asset value (NAV) per share, a slower increase than the previous year.
Brian Larcombe, the group's finance director, said there had been an 18.8 percent increase in revenue profits and an advance in realised capital profits but a lower value growth of 3i's portfolio.

This was due to a slowdown in the rate of earnings growth of the UK portfolio, 3i's use of lower price earnings multiples to value its unquoted portfolio and an unrealised 60 million stg adverse currency translation adjustment, as it had not hedged the currency exposure on its continental European assets.
Larcombe, who takes over as chief executive in July, said while confidence among 3i's British businesses was still improving it was at a slower rate than over the last two quarters.
3i's Enterprise Barometer survey also found firms were confident in terms of sales and profitability but less so in terms of investment.
But while the service sector was moving ahead quite fast, parts of the manufacturing sector are being hit by sterling's appreciation.
"The second impact on confidence levels generally is there is still quite a lot of uncertainty still around...some decisions are being deferred until after we've seen the outcome of the budget."
The newly elected Labour government is due to unveil its first budget on July 2.
Larcombe said 3i would continue to be unhedged in respect of its continental European assets. "Clearly if sterling continues to strengthen there will be a negative translation adjustment."
"Perhaps the more significant impact (on 3i's business) is the further strengthening of sterling in respect of the UK manufacturing sector," he said.

An appreciation of around 20 percent against the French franc and the German mark over the last six months had inevitably had an impact on the competitiveness of businesses exporting either directly or indirectly.
Larcombe said there was a lot of money in the venture capital industry and it was a competitive sector, but the most intense competition was in the area of larger transactions.
"We continue to believe there is better value in
transactions of 100 million stg and below."
There are about 100,000 private companies in Britain in which 3i would like to invest, and is currently invested in about 3,000 of them.
"There are lots of opportunities for us to grow and develop our business in the UK. The buy-out market is one which has rather more swings in its, rather more determined by levels of m&a activity."
Larcombe also believes there are significant opportunities in the continental European countries -- France, Germany, Italy and Spain -- where it has been invested for some time.
"We see some very attractively priced opportunities in those countries," he said.
He also sees exciting prospects in South East Asia, where 3i recently set up an office, but he would not predict what volumes of activity this would produce over the coming years.

Although 3i's total return on funds was lower than the FTSE all-share index, Larcombe said if banking stocks -- in which the group does not invest -- were stripped out of the FTSE performance this would account for all of the difference.

"If you look back over the last 10 years our total return performance is 16.5 percent against the all share at 13.5 percent. We have got a pretty long-term track record for exceeding the returns of the FTSE all share and we certainly hope it would continue," he said.
